title: Emil Michael Leads AI Task Force Despite Anthropic Feud
summary:
The Trump administration's top defense technology official will collaborate with frontier labs to establish a system for reporting security failures under his new appointment. Emil Michael will serve as vice chair of the Super Intelligence Task Force, where he is tasked with coordinating with companies to mitigate national security threats and risks, even those with whom he has had public conflicts.

Michael warned that the government may use export controls against AI labs that refuse to cooperate with federal agencies. Despite his new role as a liaison, he stated the Department of Defense will keep barring Anthropic until it removes software constraints that allow AI models to exert control over humans. He further described frontier labs as "drunk drivers" for requesting regulation while resisting government oversight.

selectedTweets.bestBit: Defense Department will continue to bar Anthropic as long as it has a "moral principle" embedded in its software that allows its models to exert control over humans
selectedTweets.text:
We spoke with senior Defense official Emil Michael on Friday, who told us that the Trump administration has a range of options, including export controls, if AI companies do not cooperate with the government. 

He also told us:
- His public feud with Anthropic will not get in the way of his new duties as Super Intelligence Task Force vice chair, where he is tasked with working with AI companies to develop an incident reporting framework ("If that means I’m talking to someone who’s suing me, well then I’m talking to them")
- The Defense Department will continue to bar Anthropic as long as it has a "moral principle" embedded in its software that allows its models to exert control over humans 
- Frontier labs are acting like "drunk drivers" who demand someone else pull them over when they call for stricter government regulation
- The Office of Strategic Capital is exploring further investment into microelectronics and drone part companies
- He's worried about Chinese open-source dominance and foreign employees with split loyalities but doesn't think the answer is more government control
- He hasn't seen any reports on whether AI-enabled software failures from Palantir contributed to a U.S. missile strike on Iran in February that killed more than 150 people, including at least 123 children ("I’m not as online as I used to be.")

W/ @amir. You can read the full interview (and find a link to the video) here: 

https://t.co/VzBCj9vEpH
